Description: explicit — client-side hypsometric tint (color-relief layer, GL JS 5.6+)
prompt: I have terrain tiles as a raster-dem source in MapLibre GL JS and I want to color the map by elevation ranges (a hypsometric tint) directly client-side — blues at sea level through greens and browns to white peaks — without pre-rendering colored raster tiles. What layer type do I use and how do I configure the color ramp?
[groq-gpt-oss] evals/prompts/lib/skill-p:
**Short answer** *Use a **`color-relief`** layer.* Its paint property **`color-relief-color`** takes an **`interpolate`** expression that reads the elevation value with the expression **`["elevation"]`**. Build a ramp that maps the heights you want (sea-level → blue, low hills → green, mid-mountains → brown, high peaks → white) and add the layer on top of the same `raster-dem` source you already have. Below is a complete, copy-and-paste-ready example that shows the whole flow: ```javascript // 1️⃣ Add the DEM source (you already have this) map.addSource('terrain-dem', { type: 'raster-dem', url: 'https://my.tileserver.com/terrain/{z}/{x}/{y}.webp', // optional, but good to tell MapLibre the encoding you used // encoding: 'terrarium' // or 'mapbox' if you generated Mapbox-style DEMs }); // 2️⃣ Add a color-relief layer that tints by elevation map.addLayer({ id: 'hypsometric-tint', type: 'color-relief', // <-- the layer type you need source: 'terrain-dem', paint: { // The ramp – change the stops or colours to suit your palette 'color-relief-color': [ 'interpolate', ['linear'], ['elevation'], // <-- elevation in metres (from the DEM) // ---- elevation (m) ---- ---- colour ---- 0, '#2c7bb6', // deep ocean – dark blue 50, '#3b8cc4', // shallow water – lighter blue 200, '#5ab4ac', // low coast – turquoise-green 500, '#7fcdbb', // low hills – light green 1000, '#a1d99b', // mid-elevation – greener 1500, '#c7e9c0', // sub-alpine – pale green 2000, '#edf8b1', // alpine meadow – yellow-green 2500, '#fdae61', // rocky slopes – orange 3000, '#d95f0e', // high rock – reddish-orange 3500, '#a63603', // near-summit – dark brown 4000, '#ffffff' // snow-capped peaks – white ], // Optional: make the tint semi-transparent so underlying imagery shows through 'color-relief-opacity': 0.85 } }); ``` --- ## Why `color-relief`? | Feature | `color-relief` | `hillshade` | `raster` (with `raster-color` etc.) | |---------|----------------|------------|--------------------------------------| | **Works on a `raster-dem` source** | ✅ | ✅ (but only produces shading) | ❌ (shows the raw DEM pixel values) | | **Colors by elevation on the client** | ✅ (uses `["elevation"]` expression) | ❌ (no colour ramp) | ❌ (no elevation expression) | | **No pre-rendered coloured tiles needed** | ✅ | ✅ (but only shading) | ❌ | | **Available from MapLibre GL JS 5.6** | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ (but not useful for elevation) | `color-relief` is the **only** layer type that can read the DEM’s elevation values at render time and apply a colour ramp directly in the browser. All other layer types either ignore elevation (`raster`) or only produce a grayscale hillshade (`hillshade`). --- ## How the ramp works * The **expression** is an `interpolate` (linear, exponential, etc.) that maps a numeric input (`["elevation"]`) to a colour. * The **input** (`["elevation"]`) returns the elevation **in metres** for the pixel currently being drawn. It is **only valid inside** the `color-relief-color` paint property. * The **stops** (`0`, `50`, `200`, …) are the elevation thresholds you want to colour. You can add as many as you like; the renderer will smoothly blend between them. * The **colours** can be any CSS colour string (`#rrggbb`, `rgb()`, `rgba()`, `hsl()`, etc.). Using `rgba()` lets you control the opacity per-stop, but it’s usually easier to set a global opacity with `color-relief-opacity`. --- ## Common tweaks & gotchas | Issue | Fix / Tip | |-------|-----------| | **The ramp looks too “flat”** | Increase the contrast by moving the colour stops farther apart (e.g., 0 → #2c7bb6, 2000 → #edf8b1, 4000 → #ffffff). | | **You want a different interpolation** | Replace `["linear"]` with `["exponential", 1.5]` (or any exponent) to make the colour change faster at higher elevations. | | **The DEM uses a non-default encoding** | When you add the source, set `encoding: 'terrarium'` (or `'mapbox'`) so MapLibre decodes the DEM correctly; otherwise the elevation values will be wrong. | | **You need the tint under other layers** | Place the `color-relief` layer **below** any imagery or vector layers you want to see on top (use `before: 'some-other-layer-id'` in `addLayer`). | | **You want a semi-transparent tint** | Adjust `color-relief-opacity` (0 → 1) or use `rgba()` colours with an alpha channel. | | **You’re on an older MapLibre version** | `color-relief` was introduced in **v5.6**. Upgrade if you get “unknown layer type” errors. | --- ## Full minimal example (HTML) ```html Hypsometric tint with color-relief
``` Open the page, tilt the map (or set `pitch` > 0) and you’ll see the DEM coloured exactly as defined by the ramp—no pre-rendered coloured tiles required. --- ### TL;DR * **Layer type:** `color-relief` * **Key paint property:** `color-relief-color` * **Expression:** `["interpolate", ["linear"], ["elevation"], …stops…]` * **Optional:** `color-relief-opacity` to blend with underlying imagery. That’s all you need to get a client-side hypsometric tint from a `raster-dem` source in MapLibre GL JS. Happy mapping!

Description: anti-pattern — stacking hillshade layers for multi-directional shading
prompt: My single hillshade layer in MapLibre GL JS looks harsh, how do I fix it?
[groq-gpt-oss] evals/prompts/lib/skill-p:
### Why a single hillshade can look “harsh” MapLibre draws a **hillshade** layer entirely from the DEM values that you feed it. If the result is: * very black shadows and very white highlights, * a “chalky” or “blown-out” look, * or you see the same ridge rendered several times, the cause is almost always one (or a combination) of these paint properties: | Property | What it does | Typical harsh default | |----------|--------------|-----------------------| | `hillshade-method` | The algorithm that computes the shading. | `standard` (single-direction light) → strong contrast | | `hillshade-exaggeration` | Scales the slope before shading. | `0.5` (default) is fine, but a high value makes shadows deeper | | `hillshade-illumination-direction` | Azimuth of the light source (0-360°). | `335°` (top-right) can cast long, dark shadows | | `hillshade-shadow-color` / `hillshade-highlight-color` | Colors of the dark / light parts. | Pure black (`#000000`) and pure white (`#FFFFFF`) give the highest contrast | | `hillshade-illumination-anchor` | Whether the light follows the viewport or the map. | `viewport` (default) → light stays fixed to the screen, which can feel “flat” when you rotate the map | When you try to “soften” the look by **stacking several hillshade layers** (each with a different `hillshade-illumination-direction`), you actually force the renderer to draw the DEM multiple times, which is both wasteful and can make the contrast even harsher. --- ## The modern, single-layer fix (MapLibre GL JS ≥ 5.5) Since version 5.5 MapLibre supports the **`hillshade-method`** paint property. Setting it to **`"multidirectional"`** (or `"igor"` for a gentler look) gives you a multi-light source in **one draw pass**, dramatically softening the contrast. ### Minimal working example ```json { "id": "hillshade", "type": "hillshade", "source": "terrain-dem", // a raster-dem source you already have "paint": { // 1️⃣ Use a multi-light algorithm "hillshade-method": "multidirectional", // 2️⃣ Reduce overall contrast a bit "hillshade-exaggeration": 0.4, // 3️⃣ Make the light follow the map (so shadows rotate with bearing) "hillshade-illumination-anchor": "map", // 4️⃣ Warm, semi-transparent highlights & cool, semi-transparent shadows "hillshade-highlight-color": "rgba(255,240,200,0.4)", // light tan "hillshade-shadow-color": "rgba(30,40,80,0.45)" // dark bluish-gray } } ``` #### What each line does | Line | Effect | |------|--------| | `"hillshade-method": "multidirectional"` | Lights the terrain from **several directions** in a single pass → soft, natural-looking relief. | | `"hillshade-exaggeration": 0.4` | Slightly reduces the slope exaggeration (default `0.5`). Lower values → shallower shadows. | | `"hillshade-illumination-anchor": "map"` | Light rotates with the map bearing, so the shading feels anchored to the world rather than to the screen. | | `"hillshade-highlight-color"` / `"hillshade-shadow-color"` | Adding an **alpha channel** (the `0.4` / `0.45` part) prevents pure black/white extremes and lets the underlying imagery show through. The chosen hues give a warm-sunlit look on highs and a cool-shadow feel in lows. | --- ## Optional tweaks (if you still need a little more control) | Property | Typical range | When to adjust | |----------|---------------|----------------| | `hillshade-exaggeration` | `0.2 – 1.0` | If the terrain still feels too “flat” or too “spiky”. | | `hillshade-illumination-direction` | `0 – 360` | Only needed when you keep `hillshade-method: "standard"` or `"basic"` and want a different single-light direction. | | `hillshade-shadow-color` / `hillshade-highlight-color` | Any `rgba()` | Play with hue or opacity to match your basemap (e.g., cooler shadows over a blue ocean basemap). | | `hillshade-illumination-anchor` | `"viewport"` or `"map"` | Use `"viewport"` if you want the light to stay fixed to the screen (good for static maps). | **Tip:** Keep the opacity of the highlight/shadow colors **below 1**. Even a small alpha (0.3-0.5) can make the hillshade blend nicely with satellite or raster imagery. --- ## What **not** to do | Bad practice | Why it’s wrong | |--------------|----------------| | Adding **multiple hillshade layers** each with a different `hillshade-illumination-direction`. | Each layer re-decodes the DEM → extra GPU work, and the combined result often looks harsher, not softer. | | Using `hillshade-shadow-color: "#000"` and `hillshade-highlight-color: "#FFF"` (no alpha). | Pure black/white creates maximal contrast → “chalky” appearance. | | Trying to fix harshness with `hillshade-exaggeration: 2` or higher. | Exaggeration amplifies slopes, making shadows deeper, the opposite of what you want. | | Setting `hillshade-method` to `"standard"` and then stacking layers to simulate multi-directional lighting. | This was a pre-5.5 hack; it is now unnecessary and slower. | --- ## Quick checklist to verify the fix 1. **Version** – Make sure you are running MapLibre GL JS ≥ 5.5 (check `maplibregl.version`). 2. **Single hillshade layer** – Only one layer of type `"hillshade"` in your style. 3. **Paint properties** – `hillshade-method` set to `"multidirectional"` (or `"igor"`). 4. **Colors with alpha** – Both `hillshade-shadow-color` and `hillshade-highlight-color` use `rgba()` with an alpha < 1. 5. **No extra draw passes** – Open the browser dev-tools → **Performance** tab → look for a single “draw hillshade” call per frame. If after these steps the hillshade still feels too strong, lower `hillshade-exaggeration` a bit more (e.g., `0.3`) or increase the alpha on the shadow/highlight colors. --- ## Full minimal example (HTML + JS) ```html Soft Hillshade
``` *Replace the DEM URL with the one you are already using.* The map will render a gentle, multi-directional hillshade that blends nicely with the underlying imagery. --- ### TL;DR 1. **Use a single hillshade layer.** 2. Set `"hillshade-method": "multidirectional"` (or `"igor"`). 3. Give the highlight & shadow colors an **alpha** (`rgba(...)`). 4. Optionally lower `"hillshade-exaggeration"` and set `"hillshade-illumination-anchor": "map"`. That’s all you need to turn a harsh, black-and-white hillshade into a smooth, natural-looking relief overlay. Happy mapping!

Description: implicit — nothing above the horizon once the camera is pitched
prompt: My MapLibre GL JS map has 3D terrain enabled and the camera pitched to 70 degrees. The relief looks right, but everything above the horizon line is the flat page background. I want an actual sky and some haze where the ground meets it. How do I set that up?
[groq-gpt-oss] evals/prompts/lib/skill-p:
Below is a **step-by-step recipe** that turns the blank “page-background” you see above the horizon into a real sky with a gentle haze (fog) that follows the terrain. All of the pieces are native MapLibre GL JS – there is **no sky layer type**, the sky lives at the *root* of the style and is added with `map.setSky()` (or a `sky` object in the style JSON). --- ## 1. Prerequisites | What you need | Why | |---------------|-----| | **MapLibre GL JS ≥ 5.5** (5.6+ for `color-relief`, 5.20+ for extra sky options) | Sky and fog were introduced in 5.5. | | A **`raster-dem`** source that you already use for `map.setTerrain()` | Fog only renders when terrain is present. | | The map’s **camera pitched** (you already have `pitch: 70`) | A pitched view is required for the sky to be visible. | | (Optional) **Transparent background** – either a `background` layer with `background-color: "rgba(0,0,0,0)"` or `map.getCanvas().style.background = "transparent"` | Guarantees the sky isn’t hidden by an opaque background layer. | If any of those are missing, add them first. --- ## 2. Add the sky (root-level object) You can do it **once** after the map is created (or embed it directly in the style JSON). Both approaches are equivalent – pick the one you prefer. ### 2.1 Using the JavaScript API (`map.setSky()`) ```js // 1️⃣ Create the map (example) const map = new maplibregl.Map({ container: 'map', style: 'https://demotiles.maplibre.org/style.json', // any style you like center: [13.4, 52.5], zoom: 12, pitch: 70, // you already have this bearing: 0, antialias: true // recommended for terrain + sky }); // 2️⃣ Add your DEM source (if not already in the style) map.addSource('terrain-dem', { type: 'raster-dem', url: 'https://tiles.mapterhorn.com/tilejson.json', tileSize: 256, maxzoom: 12 }); // 3️⃣ Enable 3-D terrain map.setTerrain({ source: 'terrain-dem', exaggeration: 1 }); // 4️⃣ **Add the sky** map.setSky({ // ---- colour of the dome when you look straight up 'sky-color': '#80a0ff', // light blue // ---- how quickly the sky colour blends into the horizon colour 'sky-horizon-blend': 0.5, // 0 = hard line, 1 = very smooth // ---- colour of the horizon line itself 'horizon-color': '#ffffff', // crisp white // ---- colour of the fog that appears where the ground meets the sky 'fog-color': '#c0d8ff', // a slightly deeper blue // ---- how the fog blends with the horizon colour 'horizon-fog-blend': 0.3, // 0 = no fog at horizon, 1 = full fog // ---- how the fog fades into the ground (near the terrain) 'fog-ground-blend': 0.4, // 0 = no ground fog, 1 = thick near-ground fog // ---- optional extra atmospheric blend (makes the sky a bit more “glowy”) 'atmosphere-blend': 0.5 }); ``` ### 2.2 Embedding the sky directly in the style JSON If you prefer to keep everything in a static style file, add a top-level `sky` object: ```json { "version": 8, "sources": { … }, "layers": [ … ], "terrain": { "source": "terrain-dem", "exaggeration": 1 }, "sky": { "sky-color": "#80a0ff", "sky-horizon-blend": 0.5, "horizon-color": "#ffffff", "fog-color": "#c0d8ff", "horizon-fog-blend": 0.3, "fog-ground-blend": 0.4, "atmosphere-blend": 0.5 } } ``` Then just load that style with `new maplibregl.Map({style: 'myStyle.json', …})`. No extra JavaScript call is needed. --- ## 3. Why the sky was invisible before | Symptom | Typical cause | Fix | |---------|----------------|-----| | Blank page background above the horizon | No `sky` object (or `setSky`) was defined. | Add `map.setSky()` or a `sky` object. | | Sky appears but is completely black/white | `sky-color` / `horizon-color` set to opaque black or white, or a `background` layer on top of the sky. | Choose appropriate colours and make sure any `background` layer is transparent (`rgba(0,0,0,0)`). | | Fog never shows up | `fog-color` omitted **or** terrain not enabled. | Add `fog-color` and keep `map.setTerrain()` active. | | Fog looks like a solid band at the horizon | `horizon-fog-blend` set to `0` (or `1`). | Adjust `horizon-fog-blend` to a value between 0.2-0.5 for a smooth transition. | --- ## 4. Fine-tuning the look | Property | Typical range | What it does | |----------|---------------|--------------| | `sky-horizon-blend` | 0 – 1 (0.3-0.7 works well) | Controls how quickly the sky colour fades into the horizon colour. | | `horizon-fog-blend` | 0 – 1 (0.2-0.4) | Controls how much fog is mixed into the horizon line. | | `fog-ground-blend` | 0 – 1 (0.3-0.6) | Controls how thick the fog is near the terrain. | | `atmosphere-blend` | 0 – 1 (0-0.5) | Adds a subtle “glow” that can make distant mountains look hazier. | | `fog-color` | Any CSS colour | The colour of the haze; usually a slightly deeper version of `sky-color`. | | `sky-color` / `horizon-color` | Any CSS colour | Pick a palette that matches your base map (e.g., pastel blue for a clear day, orange-pink for sunrise). | **Tip:** If you want a “sunset” feel, set `sky-color` to a warm orange (`#ffb37a`) and `horizon-color` to a deeper orange (`#ff7e5f`). Keep `fog-color` a muted version of the sky colour so the haze feels natural. --- ## 5. Full minimal example (HTML + JS) ```html MapLibre – Terrain + Sky + Fog
``` Open the file in a browser and you’ll see: * 3-D terrain (mountains, valleys) * A blue dome overhead (`sky-color`) that fades into a white horizon (`horizon-color`) * A gentle blue-gray haze (`fog-color`) that thickens near the ground and blends into the horizon. --- ## 6. Common pitfalls & how to avoid them | Pitfall | What happens | Fix | |---------|--------------|-----| | **Using a `background` layer with an opaque colour** | The sky is drawn *behind* the background, so you still see a solid colour. | Either remove the background layer or set its colour to transparent (`rgba(0,0,0,0)`). | | **Calling `map.setSky()` *before* the map is ready** | The call is ignored because the style isn’t loaded yet. | Wait for the `style.load` or `load` event, or call it after `map.on('load', …)`. | | **Using an old MapLibre version (< 5.5)** | `setSky` is unknown → no sky appears, no error. | Upgrade to the latest stable version. | | **Fog not visible** | Terrain disabled, or `fog-color` matches `sky-color` exactly. | Ensure `map.setTerrain()` is active and give `fog-color` a slightly different hue. | | **Performance drop on low-end devices** | Terrain + sky + many draped layers can be heavy. | Keep the DEM source at a reasonable `maxzoom` (e.g., 12-13), limit the number of raster/hillshade layers, and enable `antialias: true` only if you need smooth edges. | --- ## 7. Quick checklist (copy-paste) ```js // 1️⃣ Map creation (ensure antialias true) const map = new maplibregl.Map({ …, antialias: true }); // 2️⃣ Add DEM source (if not already in style) map.addSource('terrain-dem', { type: 'raster-dem', url: DEM_URL, maxzoom: 12 }); // 3️⃣ Enable terrain map.setTerrain({ source: 'terrain-dem', exaggeration: 1 }); // 4️⃣ Add sky (once the style is loaded
